name: Memory Safety & Exploitation
description: Memory-corruption bugs, exploitation techniques, and mitigations (ASLR, CFI, sanitizers).

ccs.narrative:
Memory safety and exploitation research at CCS has tracked the ongoing arms race between mitigations and attacker innovations. The 2018 cohort examined CFI and its limits from both sides: Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity (CCS 2018) tightened CFI by mapping each call site to a unique target, while Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks (CCS 2018) automated the construction of data-only payloads that bypass CFI entirely. Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable (CCS 2018) bridged the crash-to-exploit gap automatically.

Kernel exploitation was examined through heap manipulation: SLAKE: Facilitating Slab Manipulation for Exploiting Vulnerabilities in the Linux Kernel (CCS 2019) automated Linux slab heap grooming to enable reliable kernel exploitation. The interaction between speculation and memory safety produced Speculative Probing: Hacking Blind in the Spectre Era (CCS 2020), showing that speculative execution eliminates the need for info-leak gadgets in ASLR bypass.

Rust's memory safety guarantees were scrutinized at both the language and enclave level: Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX (CCS 2019) brought Rust's ownership model to SGX enclaves, while MirChecker: Detecting Bugs in Rust Programs via Static Analysis (CCS 2021) showed that unsafe blocks and integer overflows remain exploitable even in Rust. DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel (CCS 2022) bypassed SMEP, SMAP, and KASLR using kernel credential-object swapping.

milestones.title: Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity
milestones.note: Strengthened CFI to unique per-callsite targets, closing the over-approximation that coarse-grained CFI permits.

milestones.title: Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks
milestones.note: Automated data-only exploit construction using block-oriented programming to bypass CFI mitigations.

milestones.title: Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable
milestones.note: Automated the transformation of crash PoCs into working exploits by exploring exploitable program states.

milestones.title: SLAKE: Facilitating Slab Manipulation for Exploiting Vulnerabilities in the Linux Kernel
milestones.note: Automated Linux slab heap grooming to reliably exploit kernel heap vulnerabilities.

milestones.title: Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX
milestones.note: Applied Rust's memory-safety guarantees to SGX enclave programming to prevent memory corruption inside enclaves.

milestones.title: Speculative Probing: Hacking Blind in the Spectre Era
milestones.note: Used speculative execution to defeat ASLR without any info-leak vulnerability, fundamentally changing ASLR assumptions.

milestones.title: MirChecker: Detecting Bugs in Rust Programs via Static Analysis
milestones.note: Found exploitable bugs in Rust's unsafe code via MIR-level static analysis, showing Rust is not unconditionally safe.

milestones.title: DirtyCred: Escalating Privilege in Linux Kernel
milestones.note: Bypassed all modern Linux kernel mitigations by swapping credential kernel objects during exploitation.

ndss.narrative:
Memory safety and exploitation at NDSS has evolved from classic buffer-overflow mitigation into a broad campaign against temporal errors, information leakage, and hardware-level fault injection. IoTFuzzer (NDSS 2018) catalyzed the field by making memory corruption bugs in IoT firmware accessible to automated testing. CRCount (NDSS 2019) then addressed use-after-free errors through reference counting-based pointer invalidation, a lightweight alternative to garbage collection for systems code.

The 2020–2022 period tackled different layers of the memory-safety stack. uRAI (NDSS 2020) enforced return address integrity on embedded systems without MPU support; Refining Indirect Call Targets at the Binary Level (NDSS 2021) tightened control-flow integrity for stripped binaries; and Preventing Kernel Hacks with HAKCs (NDSS 2022) demonstrated that hardware-assisted kernel compartmentalization can limit exploit impact.

Recent work has grappled with hardware-level memory errors. Copy-on-Flip (NDSS 2023) hardened ECC memory against Rowhammer bit-flip attacks; K-LEAK (NDSS 2024) automated multi-step infoleak exploit generation for the Linux kernel; and Wallbleed (NDSS 2025) disclosed a buffer over-read in the Great Firewall of China's DNS subsystem, illustrating that memory-disclosure vulnerabilities appear even in national-scale infrastructure. The field's scope has grown from user-space heap to every software layer that touches memory.

milestones.title: IoTFuzzer: Discovering Memory Corruptions in IoT Through App-based Fuzzing
milestones.note: Discovers memory-corruption bugs in IoT devices via app-based fuzzing without requiring firmware access.

milestones.title: CRCount: Pointer Invalidation with Reference Counting to Mitigate Use-after-free in Legacy C/C++
milestones.note: Mitigates use-after-free in legacy C/C++ using reference-counting-based pointer invalidation with low overhead.

milestones.title: µRAI: Securing Embedded Systems with Return Address Integrity
milestones.note: Presents uRAI, enforcing return address integrity on microcontrollers to prevent control-flow hijacking without a shadow stack.

milestones.title: Refining Indirect Call Targets at the Binary Level
milestones.note: Refines indirect-call target sets in stripped binaries to enforce more precise control-flow integrity.

milestones.title: Preventing Kernel Hacks with HAKCs
milestones.note: Enforces kernel compartmentalization using hardware memory tagging to contain exploitation across kernel components.

milestones.title: Copy-on-Flip: Hardening ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks
milestones.note: Proposes Copy-on-Flip, a defense hardening ECC memory against Rowhammer by relocating data when bit flips are detected.

milestones.title: K-LEAK: Towards Automating the Generation of Multi-Step Infoleak Exploits against the Linux Kernel
milestones.note: Automates generation of multi-step information-leak exploits against the Linux kernel from memory errors.

milestones.title: Wallbleed: A Memory Disclosure Vulnerability in the Great Firewall of China
milestones.note: Discovers a buffer over-read memory disclosure vulnerability in the Great Firewall of China's DNS injection subsystem.

sp.narrative:
Memory safety at IEEE S&P covers both exploitation techniques and defenses against spatial and temporal memory errors. The 2018 baseline combined hardware-based defenses and DRAM attacks: Compiler-Assisted Code Randomization (S&P 2018) applied fine-grained code randomization without source access. Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses (S&P 2018) showed that hardware-refresh mitigations were insufficient against determined attackers.

2019 brought two major SoK papers that defined the field's understanding. SoK: Sanitizing for Security (S&P 2019) characterized what sanitizers—AddressSanitizer, MemorySanitizer, UBSan—actually catch and miss. SoK: Shining Light on Shadow Stacks (S&P 2019) evaluated shadow-stack implementations as a return-address protection mechanism. Exploiting Correcting Codes: On the Effectiveness of ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks (S&P 2019) showed ECC memory is a weaker Rowhammer defense than assumed.

The 2020 wave focused on temporal safety and capability architectures. Cornucopia: Temporal Safety for CHERI Heaps (S&P 2020) and Rigorous engineering for hardware security: Formal modelling and proof in the CHERI design and implementation process (S&P 2020) advanced the CHERI capability architecture. MarkUs: Drop-in use-after-free prevention for low-level languages (S&P 2020) provided a practical UAF defense without requiring recompilation.

BLACKSMITH: Scalable Rowhammering in the Frequency Domain (S&P 2022) and REGA: Scalable Rowhammer Mitigation with Refresh-Generating Activations (S&P 2023) continued the attack-defense cycle on DRAM. By 2024, the Rowhammer arms race had produced seven generations of attack and defense papers at S&P alone, reflecting DRAM's structural vulnerability as a long-lived threat surface.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here, all from USENIX 2018, frame memory safety as a two-sided arms race. On the offensive side, the community pushed hard on automation: FUZE (USENIX 2018) tackled facilitating exploit generation for kernel use-after-free bugs, while HeapHopper (USENIX 2018) brought bounded model checking to heap allocator security and Automatic Heap Layout Manipulation for Exploitation (USENIX 2018) automated the heap grooming that real exploits depend on. On the defensive side, the same year emphasized shrinking and isolating the attack surface, with Debloating Software through Piece-Wise Compilation and Loading (USENIX 2018) removing unused code and IMIX: In-Process Memory Isolation EXtension (USENIX 2018) carving out protected regions inside a process. The Guard's Dilemma (USENIX 2018) showed that even Intel SGX enclaves were not immune to efficient code-reuse attacks.

A clear shift followed in 2019-2020 toward hardware-assisted, fine-grained isolation and toward stress-testing control-flow defenses. ERIM (USENIX 2019) made in-process isolation with Intel MPK protection keys practical and efficient, and Donky (USENIX 2020) extended that protection-key model to RISC-V and x86. At the same time, defenders refined control-flow integrity with Origin-sensitive Control Flow Integrity (USENIX 2019), while CONFIRM (USENIX 2019) delivered a sobering evaluation of how compatible and relevant existing CFI protections actually were for modern software. Exploit automation kept pace through KEPLER (USENIX 2019) and KOOBE (USENIX 2020), which targeted control-flow hijacking primitives and kernel out-of-bounds writes. Crucially, this period exposed that the new isolation primitives were themselves attackable: PKU Pitfalls (USENIX 2020) demonstrated attacks on PKU-based memory isolation, foreshadowing a recurring theme.

By 2021-2022 the field had matured into a back-and-forth over both software defenses and the hardware substrate. Defensive allocator design advanced with Preventing Use-After-Free Attacks with Fast Forward Allocation (USENIX 2021), and kernel attack surface reduction continued with SHARD (USENIX 2021). But a parallel front opened around physical-layer DRAM attacks: SMASH (USENIX 2021) revived Rowhammer from JavaScript despite in-DRAM TRR mitigations, Half-Double (USENIX 2022) extended hammering to non-adjacent rows, and RETBLEED (USENIX 2022) showed arbitrary speculative code execution via return instructions. The isolation-attack theme also recurred, with Jenny (USENIX 2022) securing syscalls for PKU-based systems after earlier attacks. Most recently, ZenHammer (USENIX 2024) carried Rowhammer onto AMD Zen platforms, confirming that even as software mitigations harden, hardware-level memory corruption remains an open and evolving threat.

top4.narrative:
The earliest papers in this slice show memory-safety research branching out from the classic "corrupt memory in a desktop C/C++ program" model into new attack surfaces. A cluster of 2018 work pushed fuzzing into hard-to-reach targets, with "IoTFuzzer: Discovering Memory Corruptions in IoT Through App-based Fuzzing" (NDSS 2018) and "What You Corrupt Is Not What You Crash" (NDSS 2018) wrestling with embedded devices where crashes are silent and feedback is scarce. At the same time, the defensive community kept refining control-flow integrity and code reuse defenses — "Enforcing Unique Code Target Property for Control-Flow Integrity" (CCS 2018) and "Compiler-Assisted Code Randomization" (S&P 2018) tightened CFI and diversification — while attackers showed those defenses were not enough, with "Block Oriented Programming: Automating Data-Only Attacks" (CCS 2018) demonstrating that data-only attacks sidestep CFI entirely. A parallel "exploitability" thread emerged, where the question shifted from "is there a bug?" to "can it be weaponized?", driven by "FUZE" (USENIX 2018) for kernel use-after-free and "Revery: From Proof-of-Concept to Exploitable" (CCS 2018).

The pivotal shift came in 2019 when hardware-level flaws moved to center stage. "Spectre Attacks: Exploiting Speculative Execution" (S&P 2019) — by far the most-cited paper here — showed the CPU's own microarchitecture could leak memory across security boundaries, reframing memory safety as a hardware as well as a software problem. Rowhammer matured along the same lines: after "Another Flip in the Wall of Rowhammer Defenses" (S&P 2018), researchers broke supposedly safe configurations with "Exploiting Correcting Codes: ECC Memory Against Rowhammer" (S&P 2019) and "SPOILER" (USENIX 2019). 2019 was also a strong year for taking stock and for isolation: the SoK papers "SoK: Sanitizing for Security" (S&P 2019) and "SoK: Shining Light on Shadow Stacks" (S&P 2019) systematized the defensive toolbox, while "ERIM: Secure, Efficient In-process Isolation with Protection Keys (MPK)" (USENIX 2019) popularized cheap intra-process isolation via Intel MPK.

From 2020 onward the field consolidated around three durable themes. First, intra-process isolation became a research industry of its own — "Donky" (USENIX 2020) and "xMP" (S&P 2020) extended the MPK idea, even as "PKU Pitfalls" (USENIX 2020) showed these schemes can be attacked, mirroring the earlier attack-defense arms race in CFI. Second, trusted execution environments inherited classic memory bugs, with "A Tale of Two Worlds" (CCS 2019) and "TeeRex" (USENIX 2020) finding memory corruption inside SGX enclaves, and "Towards Memory Safe Enclave Programming with Rust-SGX" (CCS 2019) pointing to safe languages as the fix. Third, automated kernel exploitation kept advancing through "SLAKE" (CCS 2019), "KEPLER" (USENIX 2019), and "KOOBE" (USENIX 2020).

Where things stand now reflects two converging answers. On the software side, the agenda has clearly turned toward fundamentally safe foundations — hardware-enforced capabilities in "Cornucopia: Temporal Safety for CHERI Heaps" (S&P 2020) and safe-language tooling in "MirChecker: Detecting Bugs in Rust Programs via Static Analysis" (CCS 2021) — rather than only patching unsafe C. On the hardware side, the threats keep evolving faster than mitigations: Rowhammer defenses keep falling to "SMASH" (USENIX 2021), "BLACKSMITH" (S&P 2022), and "Half-Double" (USENIX 2022), and speculative execution attacks persist with "RETBLEED" (USENIX 2022). The arc of this list runs from classic software memory corruption toward an arms race that now spans the silicon itself, with safe languages and hardware capabilities as the most promising long-term escapes.
